title: How Six AWS Engineers Rebuilt Bedrock to Challenge Microsoft
content: In early 2025, things were tense inside Amazon’s cloud unit. Bedrock, a new service designed to run AI models, was proving buggy. Customers were getting error messages repeatedly and sometimes waiting weeks for the computing capacity they needed, according to people with knowledge of the customer issues. As these problems surged, a senior engineering leader, Anthony Liguori, led a team that came up with a plan for a revamped version of Bedrock—known as Project Mantle—designed to fix the throttling and error messages and enable the service to scale to serve larger numbers of users, said two of the people with direct knowledge of the situation. Liguori worked with five other senior engineers to build Mantle using AWS’ in-house AI coding tool, Kiro.

title: ElevenLabs Hires CFO, Eyes 2028 IPO
content: While all eyes are on Anthropic’s forthcoming IPO prospectus, set to drop in the coming weeks, other fast-growing AI startups are laying the groundwork for their own public offerings. The latest is AI voice startup ElevenLabs , which has hired a chief financial officer as it eyes a possible IPO in 2028. The London-based startup has tapped Ethan Tandowsky , former CFO of the $32 billion Dutch fintech firm Adyen , according to someone with direct knowledge of the hire. Tandowsky had been Adyen’s CFO since 2023, and previously held other finance posts at the company throughout its 2018 public offering. (Shares of Amsterdam-listed Adyen are up more than 80% since its IPO but has lost more than half its value since its pandemic-height.) As a refresher, ElevenLabs trains its own voice models, or AI specifically meant to generate speech from text, or vice versa. Founded in 2022 by Polish duo Mati Staniszewski and Piotr Dąbkowski , the company’s earliest customers were mostly individuals using its models to create voice-overs for YouTube videos.

title: Aviloo expands battery warranty to 26 countries - electrive.com
content:
Aviloo now offers its battery warranty for used electric cars in 26 European countries. The free coverage is linked to a qualifying flash battery test by the Austrian company.
The Urbino 18 electric buses can be charged both via a plug and a pantograph.
Image: Hyundai
Aviloo’s
battery warranty
was initially launched in June 2026 in France and Sweden, soon after adding countries such as Germany, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Austria, Finland, Belgium, Switzerland, Ireland, Norway, and Denmark. Since September, according to Aviloo, the battery warranty has also been available in the Czech Republic, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Slovakia, Iceland, Cyprus, Greece, Bulgaria, Slovenia, Luxembourg, Hungary, Poland, and Liechtenstein. The warranty is directly linked to Aviloo’s Flash Test. Any test that meets the required criteria automatically receives the battery warranty at no additional cost, the company states.
Battery warranty is linked to flash test
Using the Flash Test, Aviloo determines the State of Health (SoH) of the high-voltage battery via the OBD interface. The service targets car dealerships, used car dealers, and leasing companies, and is designed to assess the condition of a used electric vehicle’s battery independently of the manufacturer’s status display. In early September, Aviloo emphasised in its own analysis that age and mileage alone only provide limited insights into battery health. For the first
Aviloo Certified EV Battery Report
, the company evaluated more than 500,000 tests from 20 electric vehicle models, according to its own statements. The results were generally positive, finding that, after 150,000 kilometres, the median SoH of the models examined ranged between 87 and 94 per cent.
At the same time, the analysis revealed significant differences between individual vehicles of the same model. For example, with the Hyundai Ioniq 5 featuring a 72.6-kWh battery, the median SoH after 150,000 kilometres was 92.8 per cent, but the range between individual vehicles exceeded twelve percentage points. For other models, the variation was even greater.
These results thus provide the argumentative basis for Aviloo’s business model. An individual battery test is intended to provide more insight into the condition of a used electric vehicle than age and mileage alone. However, it is important to note that the underlying data comes from Aviloo itself, and the company is commercially active in battery diagnostics.
The now-expanded warranty takes a step further by combining Aviloo’s condition check with battery protection. For the used car trade in particular, such a combination could help reduce uncertainties about the condition of the vehicle’s most expensive component. Based on the information published so far, it is not yet possible to assess the extent of this protection, for which the specific warranty terms would be decisive.

title: Clarios confirms €4m-plus investments to boost EMEA sustainability and 8,000MWh savings in 2025 – Batteries International
content: Clarios has revealed investments of more than €4 million ($4.7 million) over the past year in energy-efficiency covering facilities across Europe, the Middle East and Africa as it expands sustainable production practices. Projects at the company’s plants in Hanover and Zwickau in Germany and Česká Lípa in the Czech Republic delivered combined energy savings of more than 8,000MWh in fiscal 2025, Clarios confirmed on September 7. The announcement came just weeks after the lead battery giant unveiled a major deal to source low-carbon lead for its battery manufacturing plants in the EMEA region. Clarios, which owns the VARTA Automotive brand, said the fiscal 2025 investments have sharpened its competitive advantage, while boosting reliability as a key battery supplier to vehicle manufacturers and the automotive aftermarket. A selection of the projects disclosed by the company included more than €1.3 million invested at Hanover to implement the site’s largest single energy-efficiency project — a new heat recovery system to capture previously unused waste heat from Barton reactors and mills and feed it into the plant’s internal heating network. The recovered energy is used to heat battery curing chambers and further improve energy efficiency, with an additional €1.3 million spent on modernising site equipment. At Zwickau, the battery maker has invested a total of almost €500,000 in energy recovery. Recovered heat is now used to help warm the facility, reducing overall energy consumption. The project includes upgrades to process cooling and compressed-air systems, as well as the installation of a heat-recovery system for ventilation infrastructure. Meanwhile, Clarios has invested nearly €140,000 in energy efficiency upgrades at Česká Lípa, including heat-recovery system improvements and the conversion of facility lighting to LED technology. The company said it also relies on a largely closed-loop model in production — with lead acid batteries made by Clarios designed to be 100% recyclable. Meanwhile, the firm has been showcasing its advanced battery technologies, digital and other services at the Automechanika Frankfurt trade show, ending on September 12. Werner Benade, Clarios EMEA president, said sustainable energy efficiency was a key component of securing the future of its business. “Through targeted investments, we are reducing energy demand, strengthening the resilience of our production and creating the foundation for a reliable and competitive supply of the European automotive market.” The post Clarios confirms €4m-plus investments to boost EMEA sustainability and 8,000MWh savings in 2025 appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Toyota is recalling about 10,000 C-HR EVs
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 8 2026 - 8:25 am PT
issued a recall involving around 10,000 electric C-HR vehicles. The recall stems from a potential loss of power while driving.
What to know about the Toyota C-HR EV recall
The all-electric C-HR is one of three electric SUVs Toyota now sells in North America, alongside the updated bZ and bZ Woodland.
It went on sale earlier this year, starting at about $37,000, as a smaller, sportier alternative to
, Toyota’s first electric SUV.
While the new C-HR EV is off to a promising start, the electric crossover is already facing its first recall.
Toyota issued a safety recall involving certain model-year 2026 C-HR vehicles in North America. While details are still limited at this point, Toyota said about 10,000 C-HR models are involved in the recall.
The issue stems from a software glitch with the regenerative braking system. Under certain conditions, when the battery is fully charged or has a high charge level, the regenerative braking system can overcharge it.
Toyota C-HR EV (Source: Toyota)
When this happens, the electric drive system can shut down, causing the vehicle to lose power while driving.
Owners of affected vehicles can take them to a Toyota dealership, where technicians will update the battery ECU (electronic control unit) software.
2026 Toyota C-HR EV XSE interior (Source: Toyota)
Toyota will notify owners in early November 2026. The recall has not yet been released on the
website, so details are still limited. We should learn more soon. Check back for the latest updates.
In the meantime, owners can contact Toyota’s Brand Engagement Center at 1-800-331-4331. To see whether your vehicle is involved, visit
or, when it becomes available, nhtsa.gov/recalls and enter your VIN or license plate number.
Only the 2026 C-HR model year is affected. The
2027 Toyota C-HR
is also on sale now.

title: Tesla Cybercab has a hidden virtual joystick to drive it manually
content:
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 8 2026 - 7:48 am PT
A Tesla Cybercab rider found something in the robotaxi: a manual driving mode. When he got in, the touchscreen was showing a virtual joystick to drive the car by hand.
Tesla built the Cybercab with no steering wheel and no pedals. But it apparently still has a way to drive it manually, and you do it by dragging a finger across a screen.
Matthew Skrzypczak posted a video on X on September 7 showing his Cybercab in an unusual state.
“When I got in the vehicle, the display was in a different configuration with a virtual joystick for manual driving,” he wrote, adding that he had “a feeling I wasn’t supposed to see this” and then tried to drive the car with it anyway.
#cybercab
situation! When I got in the vehicle, the display was in a different configuration with a virtual joystick for manual driving! I have a feeling I wasn’t supposed to see this… but I try to manually drive the vehicle anyway! 😂
@wholemars
@DirtyTesLa
@DavidMoss
The clip shows the Cybercab’s single touchscreen split in two. The left side is a driving interface built around an on-screen joystick, with a prompt to “Close cabin doors” and buttons for opening the doors and calling support. The right side shows a live surround-camera view of the car parked in what looks like a parking lot – though the side cameras appear to be frozen on a frame from a previous location at a Supercharger.
What it shows is the workaround Tesla built for a car with no physical controls. A Cybercab still has to be moved by a person sometimes, whether that’s repositioning it in a depot or nudging it out of a tight spot, and with no wheel and no pedals, an on-screen joystick is how you do it. Tesla has never shown this mode publicly.
A robotaxi with “almost” no controls
Tesla launched the Cybercab in Austin on September 3, and that same day
NHTSA opened an audit
into how it certified a vehicle with no steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors. The agency wants to know whether Tesla was right to decide that certain federal safety standards simply don’t apply to a driverless car. That probe covers roughly 1,000 vehicles.
The pitch has always been that the Cybercab doesn’t need manual controls because it drives itself. Yet here’s manual control, buried in a menu.
And Tesla has already left the door open to more. Back in October, chair Robin Denholm
said the car could get real controls
if it had to: “If we have to have a steering wheel, it can have a steering wheel and pedals.”
We have seen many Cybercab prototypes equipped with a steering wheel and pedals during the test phase.
Electrek’s Take
A touchscreen joystick is fine for creeping a car across a parking lot at walking speed, but those controls honestly look awful to use. It’s not a serious answer to the question regulators are actually asking, which is what happens when a driverless car needs a human and there’s no real way for one to take over.
Tesla removed the wheel and pedals to make a point, that full autonomy is here and manual controls are obsolete. And yet, it has yet to scale its robotaxi service, which has been in operation for more than year with Model Ys, which use the same autonomous hardware and software as the Cybercab, which is ultimately just a different form factor.

title: BYD's top-selling 1,100+ hp luxury GT is about to get a bit cheaper
content:
Peter Johnson
| Sep 8 2026 - 7:02 am PT
is launching a new Denza Z9 GT model on September 9. The new tri-motor variant is expected to start at around $50,000, filling the gap between the current range-topping Performance and Flagship RWD models.
BYD adds new tri-motor Denza Z9 GT model
revealing the new Z9 GT
earlier this year, BYD’s luxury sub-brand, Denza, claimed it was the “world’s longest pure electric driving range electric vehicle,” delivering a CLTC range of up to 1,036 km (643 miles).
The electric GT was among BYD’s first vehicles to use its latest Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, enabling the battery to recharge from 10% to 70% in as little as 5 minutes.
It’s available in both fully electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) versions with single- or tri-motor configurations.
The single-motor Denza Z9 GT variant features a rear-mounted electric motor with 370 kW (496 hp), while the tri-motor model packs a combined 850 kW (1,140 hp) based on BYD’s e3 platform.
Measuring 5,195 mm in length, 1,990 mm in width, and 1,480 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 3,125 mm, the Denza Z9 GT is about the size of a Porsche Panamera.
Denza Z9 GT (Source: Li Hui)
According to Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, the new Z9 GT has been China’s top-selling luxury GT for several consecutive months. However, in response to customer feedback, Li confirmed that a new all-electric Denza Z9 GT model will launch on September 9.
The new variant will be a “lighter” tri-motor EV configuration, while “exciting purchase incentives” will also be available.
Denza Z9 GT interior (Source: Denza)
While no other details were revealed, the new Denza Z9 GT is expected to fill the gap between the most expensive e3 Performance and Flagship RWD models.
The Denza Z9 GT Flagship RWD starts at 299,800 yuan ($44,500) while the e3 Performance starts at 369,800 yuan ($55,000), meaning the new tri-motor variant will likely start at around 339,800 yuan, or about $50,000.
Denza Z9 GT (Source: Denza)
BYD also sells the
Denza Z9 GT in Europe
, starting at €115,000 ($134,500) in Germany. Orders initially opened in bigger markets like Germany, France, Italy, Spain, and the UK, but BYD said it would expand to 30 countries by the end of 2026.
Whether or not BYD will launch the new lower-priced tri-motor model in Europe has yet to be confirmed.
We should learn more on September 9, when the new variant goes on sale in China. Check back on Wednesday for a full breakdown.

title: Plug-in Hybrids emit 6x more pollution than claimed, and they're getting dirtier
content:
A new study shows that the gap between real-world pollution from plug-in hybrids and official government estimates is getting wider – and worse, plug-in hybrids themselves are getting dirtier.
And the car lobby is trying to hide it, and make it harder to regulate the pollution coming out of these vehicles.
The evolution of transportation takes many forms, and we here at Electrek like to cover most of them. It leads to all sorts of weird acronyms – BEV, PHEV, EREV, FCEV, HEV and so on.
Here, we’re talking about the PHEVs. Plug-in hybrid vehicles.
PHEVs are cars that have a significantly sized battery which can be filled up by plugging in, unlike conventional hybrids, which get all their energy from gasoline and merely recapture some of it during braking. Some have bigger batteries than others, but most of them can run on pure battery mode at least for some reasonable number of miles.
Plug-in hybrids are often thought of as a “transitional” technology between fully fossil-powered vehicles and fully electrically-powered ones, because you can use either as a fuel source. More flexibility means you can use whatever fuel source is more convenient for your current application.
It seems like a “best of both worlds” situation at first look… but there are downsides. PHEVs are more mechanically complex, and often one or both of the powertrains will be cobbled together as an afterthought, leading to a compromised vehicle overall.
And then, there’s the pollution, which turns out to be far higher in the real world than anyone wants to admit.
We’ve covered many, many studies showing that PHEVs are dirtier than expected, and now Transport & Environment (T&E) is out with a new update showing that not only is the gap between real-world and laboratory emissions growing for EU PHEVs, but PHEVs are getting dirtier over time, rather than cleaner.
PHEVs are now 6x dirtier than testing indicates
The analysis is an update of T&E’s previous work, showing a trend of PHEV emissions testing estimates getting less and less realistic over time.
The new update uses data from 220,000 PHEVs in Europe. Europe has mandated fuel use monitoring on vehicles, called the “On Board Fuel Consumption Monitoring” (OBFCM) system. This allows for much better real-world data, which can then be compared against laboratory data to see how cars use fuel in the real world, rather than tests (which, as we have learned, can be gamed).
T&E analyzed this data and found that PHEV emissions rose from 138 gCO2/km in 2023 to 145 gCO2/km in 2024, an increase of 5% in a year. Needless to say, this is going in the wrong direction.
In fact, 145 gCO2/km is only 14% less than the average for fossil-fueled vehicles, meaning in the real world, PHEVs are only barely cleaner.
Not only is this going in the wrong direction, but government testing indicated over the same period that PHEVs should have gotten cleaner. But in the real world, they didn’t. So what’s going on here?
It’s about “utility factors”
Since PHEVs have two powertrains with vastly different pollution profiles (one of which produces no tailpipe pollution, and one which is responsible for the hurricanes and wildfires ravaging the planet and millions of deaths per year), any testing has to estimate how often you’re going to use each of those powertrains.
So government includes a “utility factor” calculation for how often it thinks battery power will be used. And those utility factors are way, way off.
It turns out that people just don’t plug PHEVs in. (Although, that said, even when running on electric mode, PHEVs use 3x more gas than claimed)
This happens for various reasons, and the amount that it happens differs from territory to territory and from car to car. But in every study we’ve seen, whether in EU (where OBFCM data is available, and thus these studies are more common) or in the USA, the common fact is that tests always underestimate the pollution that PHEVs put out. On the better-designed PHEVs, if you do plug them in all the time, they can be much cleaner than a gas car… but people just don’t do it.
Car lobby wants to keep numbers wrong to keep selling you engines
With all these studies showing PHEVs to be dirtier than we thought, it would make sense for government to act and fix the estimates (and for automakers to make PHEVs that are more worth plugging in, as some of the above-linked studies have suggested).
Updating testing is precisely the plan – as the gap between testing and real-world emissions has been rising, the EU has planned to update “utility factors” to better reflect the reality of how people use their vehicles.
But the problem with that is that if Europe finally more realistically accounts for the real-world pollution coming out of these vehicles, auto manufacturers wouldn’t be able to get as much unearned “extra credit” for selling polluting gas-powered cars with a small battery and plug attached. This would be a threat to their greenwashing, and they can’t have it.
So automakers have consistently lobbied the EU to weaken updates to utility factors, which would allow their vehicles to continue polluting, but allow them to continue patting themselves on the back for greening their fleet when they have done no such thing.
Test numbers don’t matter, the real harm done is what matters
To be clear: pollution matters in the real world because of the health problems it causes for everyone, and because of its contribution to climate change. Neither of those damages care about what the gamed testing numbers say. If you breathe pollution, you breathe it either way, even if the automakers lie to you and tell you that the air was clean.
We’ve been through something similar before – Dieselgate. In that instance, VW (and, uh, basically everyone else) lied to the tests while polluting more in the real world. This is part of why we have OBFCM in the first place – so we don’t have to rely on the tests, and we can know what’s going on in the real world. And here we are, just a decade later, falling to the same lies.
Top comment by Spencer Hodges
The technical reason is two fold. First, yes people don't actually plug them in as expected. But this just turns them into a conventional hybrid. And hybrids pollute more than expected largely because of the catalytic converter not maintaining operational temperatures. At its operational temp of hundreds of degrees Celsius, it can be >90% efficient in conversion of NOx, HC and CO. But during the warm up period, the catalyst barely does anything. And in hybrids, it's possible for the catalyst to never reach operational temperatures. It's a real problem.
Further, as pointed out by Lucien Mathieu from T&E, these sorts of delays harm the European auto industry.
“Plug-in hybrids are one of the auto industry’s greatest greenwashing stunts – marketed as a green solution, yet delivering a heavy environmental toll in practice. They are also a major rip-off for consumers, who end up paying far more for fuel than expected. Carmakers are demanding that the EU turn a blind eye so it can delay investing in fully electric cars. Utility factors were designed to make official emission match with real-world; they are evidence-based policy making. If Europe wants to keep a chance to compete with China in the global EV race, it must resist any attempt to weaken the utility factors.”
Automakers have used this PHEV “extra credit” to delay deploying pure EV cars – they’ll add a small battery to an ICE car, get bonus points for doing very little, and continue on without updating their cars to what the state of the art of the industry can actually provide. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are rapidly deploying new EVs, and those are gaining share in Europe and across the glove rapidly, displacing European-made cars. If Europe wants to keep up, it needs to stop deluding itself and start confronting reality.
Can we please learn a lesson for once, and stop trusting the automakers when we know they’re lying?

title: Polestar confirms Formula 2030 concept previewing next Polestar 2 and 7
content:
Polestar
Polestar 2
Fred Lambert
| Sep 8 2026 - 5:42 am PT
The Polestar Formula 2030 concept car. Source: Polestar
Polestar has confirmed a new concept car, the Formula 2030, and it’s the clearest look yet at where the Swedish EV brand’s design is headed.
The concept previews styling that will show up on the next Polestar 2, due in 2027, and the Polestar 7 compact SUV coming in 2028. It’s also the design centerpiece of a broader strategy the company is pitching to investors around one goal: getting to profit.
A bold evolution, not a redesign
The Formula 2030 is the first full design statement from Philipp Romers, who
took over as Polestar’s head of design
in 2024 after arriving from Audi and replacing Maximilian Missoni.
Romers isn’t tearing up the playbook. “It was obvious we needed a bold evolution not revolution of what came before,” he said, pointing to the “Dual Blade” headlights that stay front and center on the concept so it “remains recognizably a Polestar.”
The Formula 2030 previews the design of the next Polestar 2 and Polestar 7. Source: Polestar
You can see it in the images. The front end keeps the split-blade light signature Polestar has run since the Polestar 2, and the profile is the same low, long-roof fastback shape the brand has leaned on. This is a refinement of a look that’s already on the road, not a reinvention.
That’s a reasonable call. Polestar’s design has always been one of its stronger cards, and the company doesn’t have the money right now to gamble on a radical reset.
Tied to the “Formula 2030” strategy
Polestar didn’t reveal the concept at a motor show. It showed it behind closed doors to investors, retailers, and a group of VIP customers at “The Cube,” its Gothenburg headquarters, as part of a “Formula 2030 strategy event.”
Polestar showed the concept at a strategy event at its Gothenburg HQ. Source: Polestar
The concept is being sold internally as proof the product pipeline is on track, and it’s landing at a moment when Polestar badly needs that story to hold up. The company says the strategy is meant “to continue business growth and drive to profitability.”
The showcar gets its public debut later this year, riding along with the media launch of the Polestar 4 SUV.
The numbers behind the pitch
Polestar is coming off a record first half on volume and a still-ugly bottom line. It delivered 30,423 vehicles in H1 2026, its best-ever first half, but posted a net loss of $842 million on revenue of $1.36 billion, which was down 4% year over year. Gross margin sat at -8%.
The losses are narrowing, which is the point Polestar wants investors focused on. The H1 net loss shrank 29% from a year earlier, and the company has been cutting the gap for several quarters. But it’s still losing money on every car at the gross level, and it recently trimmed its full-year delivery guidance.
There’s also a hole in the map. Polestar effectively lost the US market after it was
barred from selling there under the federal Chinese-connected-vehicle rule
, which hits cars with Chinese software and manufacturing ties. That’s a big chunk of premium-EV demand the brand now can’t touch, and it makes Europe the center of the whole plan.
The next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7 are the two products meant to carry that plan. Polestar has said the
7 will replace the 2 as its entry point
and target Europe’s largest EV segment, and it’s part of a wave of
four new models the company is pushing out over three years
Electrek’s Take
A design concept is the cheapest, safest thing a struggling automaker can put out, and I don’t mean that as an insult. Polestar can’t afford a splashy new factory reveal or a moonshot product right now, so showing off a sharp evolution of a design language people already like is their move to play.
The substance is still the next Polestar 2 and the Polestar 7. Those are the cars that decide whether “Formula 2030” is a real turnaround or a nice slide deck.
The trend line is going the right way. Losses are shrinking, H1 volume was a record, and the product cadence is genuinely aggressive for a company this size. But “drive to profitability” has been the plan for years, and the goalpost keeps moving.
The good news is that Geely doesn’t appear to be giving up on Polestar.

title: ENGWE’s new E26 3.0 e-bike packs dual motors, full suspension, and half a deer
content:
Micah Toll
| Sep 8 2026 - 3:22 am PT
ENGWE has just launched its latest all-terrain electric bike, the E26 3.0, and the company is going big on power this time around. The new model combines dual hub motors, full suspension, and chunky fat tires into a bike that looks designed to handle just about anything you can throw at it.
While ENGWE has plenty of
commuter-focused models
, this new launch appears to be designed for the dirt – and has the power to match it.
The ENGWE E26 3.0 uses a pair of hub motors rated for a combined 2,000W of peak power, with ENGWE claiming up to 160 Nm of torque.
That dual-motor setup gives riders the option of putting down considerably more power than you’d find on a typical commuter-oriented electric bicycle, especially when climbing loose or steep terrain.
I assume there’s some AI at work in this marketing image, or else they’re coming back for the rest of the deer later
The top speed is listed at 28 mph (45 km/h) on throttle and 31 mph (50 km/h) under pedal assist.
Stored power comes from a fairly sizable 48V and 20Ah battery, giving the bike 960Wh of capacity. ENGWE claims up to 100 miles (161 km) of range when using a single motor in the lowest pedal assist setting, or 70 miles (113 km) with both motors active. As usual, those are best-case figures, and riders making liberal use of both motors should expect significantly less range. Either way you slice it though, that’s still a pretty big battery.
It’s worth pointing out that the E26 3.0’s dual-motor power level and top speeds on both throttle and pedal assist put it outside the typical Class 1/2/3 e-bike framework used across much of the US. Riders should check their local and state regulations to determine where a bike with this level of performance can legally be ridden.
That distinction may be somewhat less important for the type of riding ENGWE appears to be targeting here. The E26 3.0 is clearly positioned as an all-terrain machine, and on private property or other areas without e-bike classification restrictions, its street-legal classification isn’t necessarily as critical as it would be for a bike primarily designed for commuting. Public trails are another matter, of course, particularly those that specifically restrict access to Class 1, 2, or 3 e-bikes.
The rest of the bike is similarly geared toward all-terrain riding. There are 26 x 4-inch puncture-resistant fat tires, a 120mm travel front suspension fork, and 80mm of adjustable rear air suspension. Hydraulic disc brakes with large 203mm rotors provide the stopping power.
There’s also a 3.5-inch full-color display, integrated LED lighting, rear rack, and a claimed payload capacity of 400 lb (181 kg). At 85.9 lb (39 kg), though, this definitely isn’t the kind of e-bike you’re going to enjoy carrying up a flight of stairs. Even getting it into the back of a truck is going to either be a partner job or a concerted effort with some focused bracing.
The ENGWE E26 3.0 is
launching at $1,799
, discounted from a listed $2,399 MSRP. At that price, you’re getting an impressive amount of hardware: dual motors, nearly 1 kWh of battery, full suspension, hydraulic brakes, fat tires, and a fender package.
It’s certainly not a lightweight or subtle e-bike, but that’s not really the point. ENGWE appears to have built the E26 3.0 for riders who would rather have too much motor than not enough – and for
, they’re getting quite a lot of it. Just remember to ride it where you’re permitted!

title: EU deploys 33.8 GW of solar in H1 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
SolarPower Europe expects the EU to install 68.1 GW of solar capacity in 2026, just 2.1% below the record 69.6 GW added in 2025. The outlook has improved since December, but policy uncertainty, reduced support and grid constraints continue to pose risks to growth.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
The Núñez de Balboa solar plant in Spain
The European Union’s solar market continued to grow in the first half of 2026, with at least 33.8 GW of new capacity installed between January and June. The figure represents a 1.9% increase from the 33.2 GW deployed during the same period in 2025, according to SolarPower Europe’s
EU Solar Market Update 2026: Mid-Year Analysis
The result exceeded forecasts published in late 2025 that had pointed to a market contraction, but does not yet indicate a clear acceleration in growth. Demand remained resilient despite worsening market conditions, supported in part by renewed concerns over fossil fuel supplies stemming from the conflict in the Middle East. Higher energy prices and energy security concerns have strengthened the economic case for solar across several EU member states.
Germany and Spain, the EU’s two largest markets, maintained high installation levels, while France, Italy, Poland, Romania, and Greece recorded slight year-on-year growth. Some smaller markets, such as Finland and Latvia, experienced rapid expansion driven by the commissioning of large-scale photovoltaic projects.
Conversely, the Netherlands, Czechia, Belgium, and Hungary fell short of the levels recorded in 2025. The structure of the European market is not expected to change significantly during 2026: utility-scale projects will account for approximately 56% of new capacity, compared to 44% for rooftop installations. Within the latter segment, residential demand weakened in several markets, whereas the commercial and industrial segment demonstrated greater resilience.
Photovoltaics reduce the gas bill
Beyond the growth in installed capacity, solar generation is playing an increasingly strategic role in European energy security. In the six months following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East — starting March 1 — EU solar generation is estimated to have avoided around €30 billion in gas import costs for electricity generation, equivalent to more than €1 billion per week.
Photovoltaics met over 20% of the EU’s electricity demand in May, June, and July, reaching a record 25% in June, when it became the Union’s primary source of electricity generation.
High solar output also helped meet the increased demand for cooling during summer heatwaves. During these months, high river temperatures and low water levels limited the availability of nuclear and hydroelectric power generation.
The association notes that these factors are reshaping the role of photovoltaics within the European electricity system. “In addition to being a key technology for decarbonization, solar power is establishing itself as an energy security asset capable of reducing Europe’s exposure to fossil fuel imports,” explains SolarPower Europe.
Bottlenecks
However, the growth of photovoltaics is highlighting the limitations of Europe’s electricity infrastructure. Rising renewable energy curtailment, falling solar capture prices, episodes of negative pricing, and increased price spikes during evening hours indicate that grids, storage, and other flexibility mechanisms are not keeping pace with the expansion of solar generation.
“Without a faster rollout of these technologies, Europe risks wasting an increasing share of low-cost solar electricity during the middle of the day and subsequently remaining dependent on expensive fossil-fuel generation when solar output drops,” the report states.
Outlook for 2026
The outlook for 2026 has improved substantially. SolarPower Europe’s central scenario now projects 68.1 GW of new solar capacity in the EU this year, 6.6 GW above its December 2025 forecast and just 2.1% below the revised 2025 record of 69.6 GW.
Uncertainty remains high, however. The association’s low scenario puts new installations at 62 GW, while its high scenario projects 74.1 GW. The final figure will depend on market developments in the second half of the year and potential revisions to preliminary installation data.
Meanwhile, reduced policy support in several member states, growing regulatory uncertainty and grid constraints continue to pose structural risks to market growth.

title: France seeks recyclers for CdTe, CIGS solar modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Soren is seeking companies to develop thin-film PV module recycling solutions in France for CdTe and CIGS technologies, with proposals due Oct. 21, 2026. The selected solution will prioritize a 1,300-tonne batch of CdTe modules as recycling volumes are projected to rise sharply through 2037.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Soren de Galloo Halluin reprocessing site
, the government-approved eco-organization responsible for collecting and processing end-of-life photovoltaic modules in France, has launched a
call for expressions of interest
(CEI) to identify companies capable of developing and deploying a processing solution in France for thin-film PV modules.
The initiative targets cadmium telluride (CdTe) and copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) technologies, while the ability to process amorphous silicon (a-Si) modules would be considered an advantage.
The deadline for submissions is Oct. 21, 2026. Only candidates that participate in the CEI and meet the eligibility criteria will be able to submit proposals under the subsequent call for projects.
Priority processing for 1,300 tonnes of CdTe modules
The proposed processing solutions do not need to be dedicated exclusively to end-of-life PV modules, but they must be able to handle modules from different manufacturers within the same technology category.
Once a processing solution becomes operational, a 1,300-tonne batch of CdTe modules produced by German manufacturer
will be prioritized for processing.
In 2026, Soren commissioned the Becquerel Institute to assess the potential volumes of PV modules requiring processing in France and Europe. The study was based on a literature review and interviews with PV industry stakeholders, including module manufacturers, project developers and PV waste management companies.
According to the study, the volume of CdTe modules that Soren could be required to process in France is estimated at 770 tonnes in 2027, rising to 2,660 tonnes in 2030 and 15,000 tonnes in 2037.
For CIGS modules, the corresponding volumes are estimated at 430 tonnes in 2027, 1,090 tonnes in 2030 and 2,900 tonnes in 2037.

title: UK grid connections reform mishandled, regulator finds - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Reform of Great Britain’s grid connections queue missed deadlines and was marred by inaccurate offers, poor developer engagement and digitalization issues, according to Ofgem. The regulator nevertheless found NESO delivered a “good performance” overall, meeting or exceeding expectations in seven of eight performance obligations.
Matthew Lynas
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Reform of Great Britain’s connections queue failed on multiple counts, according to the latest regulator assessment of grid operator NESO’s performance. The assessment confirms issues UK developers have been highlighting throughout the process.
NESO has been engaged in reform to change Great Britain’s grid connection queue from a first come, first served methodology to a first ready, first served approach that takes consideration of system needs.
The grid operator was successful in significantly reducing an oversubscribed queue, including clearing 153 GW of battery energy storage system capacity. However, developers have been sounding alarm bells over the challenges the process presented, previously telling
pv magazine
that data issues have meant more work, while a lack of transparency made decision making hard.
In an interview in the
September issue of pv magazine Global,
Solar Energy UK chief executive Chris Hewett commented: “On the one hand, we’ve had connection reform and lots of people have offers. Lots of those offers are way higher than they were expecting, and some of them are wrong, and some are millions of pounds in excess of what they were suggested.”
Ofgem has now confirmed much of what developers said in its latest assessment of NESO’s performance. The regulator’s report examining NESO’s performance during the period 2025 to 2026 found the grid operator had failed to implement connections reform on time, had missed deadlines, and had distributed inaccurate connection offers during the process.
Engagement with developers was also described as poor, and issues with digitalization including the rollout of an online connections portal – which Ofgem described as critical for delivery – experiencing multiple technical and usability challenges that “could have been mitigated at the time.”
Connections reform was just one element of the grid operator’s performance under assessment. Overall, Ofgem found that NESO had delivered a “good performance” against the majority of its objectives, meeting or exceeding expectations in seven of the eight performance obligations set by the regulator. However, Ofgem described connections reform as a “critical” performance objective.
In response to the findings, Zoe Morrisey, director of legal and regulation at NESO, noted that Ofgem’s overall conclusion was that “NESO met expectations.” In a blog post on the grid operator’s website, Morrisey noted the assessment covered the NESO’s first full financial year. NESO was formed in October 2024 when the British government acquired the electricity system operator from National Grid plc.
The legal director acknowledged that the section on connections reform “made for difficult reading.”
“The transformation of the grid connections process has not been easy and we accept that, though it is a shared endeavor across government, Ofgem the networks and NESO, the journey has been harder than it should have been.
“We also recognize Ofgem’s feedback that we must find a clearer way of demonstrating value for money, particularly at a time where energy costs are high. We have not waited for this feedback to act – we are already taking steps to strengthen performance in both areas.” Morrisey said.

title: Solarworld, Rays Power plan 2.4 GW solar cell factory in India - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Solarworld Energy Solutions and Rays Power Infra have formed a 50:50 joint venture to build a 2.4 GW n-type TOPCon solar cell factory in Madhya Pradesh, India.
The $105.5 million facility is expected to begin commercial production in June 2027.
Uma Gupta
08 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Highlights
solar cells
Solarworld Energy Solutions
Rays Power Infra
have formed a 50:50 joint venture to set up a 2.4 GW solar cell manufacturing facility in the Indian state of Madhya Pradesh.
The facility will be developed through Rays Green Energy Manufacturing, in which Solarworld and Rays Power will each hold a 50% stake. The companies recently signed a securities subscription agreement and joint venture agreement with Rays Green Energy Manufacturing.
The factory will be built on a 41.3-acre site at Mohasa-Babai in Narmadapuram district. It will produce n-type TOPCon G12R solar cells, with commercial production scheduled to start in June 2027.
Solarworld said the project will provide a backward-integration platform for solar cell manufacturing and strengthen its solar value chain. It said the facility will help secure long-term cell supplies, reduce reliance on third-party suppliers, and complement its existing solar engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and module manufacturing operations.
The project is expected to cost INR 10 billion ($105.5 million).
Solarworld said the aggregate financial commitment under the agreements is up to INR 5.2 billion ($54.9 million). This includes an equity investment of up to INR 2 billion ($21.1 million) in Rays Green Energy Manufacturing, with Solarworld and Rays Power each contributing up to INR 1 billion ($10.5 million). Solarworld will also provide Rays Green Energy Manufacturing with a loan of up to INR 3.2 billion ($33.8 million) to finance the project.

title: Togo kicks off solar tender - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Togo is tendering a solar project to be built in the northern part of its capital, Lomé. The planned capacity of the plant has not been disclosed. The deadline for prequalification is September 15.
Patrick Jowett
08 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
The Togolese Agency for Rural Electrification and Renewable Energies has administered a tender for a new solar power plant.
The project is set to be built in Agoe Nyive, a prefecture in the northern part of Lomé, capital of Togo.
Available tender details
state the selected developer will be responsible for the design, supply, construction and commissioning of the solar power plant, as well as the operation and maintenance for three years after commissioning. The planned capacity of the solar plant has not been disclosed.

The tender opens with a prequalification round. Prospective applicants can purchase a complete set of the prequalification documents for a non-refundable fee of XOF 100,000 ($177.32).
Applications for prequalification must be delivered via sealed envelope to the agency by September 15.
This latest tender in Togo follows an opportunity to
construct solar minigrids
in 27 rural localities across the country, which closed for applications in May.
The Africa Solar Industry Association (AFSIA) has identified 654.7 MW of operational solar projects in Togo, according to its project database, the majority of which is unidentified C&I projects.
The country’s largest operational solar project is the Blitta solar PV plant, developed by Amea Power. It was originally commissioned at 50 MW but has since been expanded to a total capacity of 70 MW.

title: South Korea to expand renewable monitoring mandate to 20 kW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The South Korean government says it will require far smaller solar, wind and fuel-cell installations to carry real-time monitoring and remote-control capability from 2027, easing the switch to commercial mobile networks along the way.
Brian Publicover
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Monitoring
South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment (MCEE) will require solar, wind, and fuel-cell installations as small as 20 kW to carry real-time monitoring and remote-control capability from 2027. It said the change also eases the switch to commercial mobile networks.
The MCEE said it revised its transmission and distribution regulations on Sept. 4, expanding the equipment mandate to cover business-use and electricity-trading solar, wind and fuel-cell installations of 20 kW or more. The equipment gives operators real-time visibility into output and operating status and allows remote adjustment of generation during voltage spikes or grid faults.
The ministry said generation operators will now be permitted to use commercial 4G LTE mobile networks rather than being required to connect through Korea Electric Power Corp.’s (Kepco) proprietary e-WSN utility communications network. Kepco is South Korea’s national electric utility.
The MCEE estimated the switch will reduce equipment costs from about KRW 4.6 million ($3,420) to about KRW 2 million per installation, a 57% reduction, and cut commissioning time from about 84 days to about 10 days, an 88% reduction.
Under current rules, generation operators bear the full cost of building monitoring and control systems, with costs rising in mountainous or remote areas that require wired cable, and Kepco’s e-WSN network taking an average of three months to connect.
The MCEE said the mandate builds on a rollout that began in October 2020, when it first required monitoring and control equipment for new solar, wind and fuel-cell installations of 100 kW or more on Jeju Island, before gradually widening the scope.
An official from the MCEE’s power grid policy bureau said in a statement that the revision lays the groundwork for grid stability as renewable capacity expands, and that the ministry will continue pursuing grid-stability measures to reach its 2030 target.
According to South Korea’s First Renewable Energy Basic Plan, the country aims to raise renewable capacity from about 37 GW in 2025 to 100 GW by 2030, 163 GW by 2035, and 220 GW by 2040.
The monitoring mandate follows other recent MCEE moves to modernize South Korea’s grid ahead of that expansion. The ministry earmarked KRW 321 billion for
distributed-grid upgrades
in 2026, including 85 new energy storage systems by 2030. And in July, it secured KRW 558.6 billion over five years for its first
distribution-line ESS program
, which Energy Minister Kim Sung-hwan said would help resolve distribution-network bottlenecks as renewables become a primary power source.

title: HiNa Battery scales Korean sodium-ion partnership from 15 MWh to 10 GWh - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
HiNa Battery signed a five-year deal to supply South Korea’s Volta with 10 GWh of sodium-ion batteries, expanding an earlier 15 MWh storage partnership. The agreement highlights sodium-ion technology’s shift toward GWh-scale energy storage deployments, though LFP batteries remain dominant in the market.
Vincent Shaw
08 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Chinese sodium-ion battery manufacturer HiNa Battery has signed a five-year agreement with South Korea’s Volta Co. for the supply of 10 GWh of sodium-ion batteries, marking a significant expansion of the companies’ existing cooperation.
The strategic agreement was signed on Sept. 2 and builds on an earlier 15 MWh storage program involving utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential applications, according to HiNa Battery. The company did not disclose the contract value, annual delivery schedule or timing of the first shipments.
Under the cooperation framework, HiNa Battery will provide sodium-ion cell technology and manufacturing capacity, while Volta will lead energy storage system integration and market development in South Korea. Kwangwoon University will participate as a technical verification partner, providing research, testing and validation support.
The arrangement creates a three-party structure combining Chinese cell manufacturing with local system integration and independent technical verification. HiNa said the earlier 15 MWh program provided the application basis for expanding cooperation to the five-year supply framework. Public information on the validation projects remains limited, with no detailed disclosure of their locations, individual capacities, cell configurations or operating data.
HiNa Battery, whose technology originated from sodium-ion research led by Hu Yongsheng at the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Physics, has been one of China’s early commercial developers of sodium-ion batteries.
Its current storage products include the HE240, a 240 Ah cell designed primarily for large-scale storage, and the NE170, a 170 Ah product targeting frequency regulation and distributed storage. HiNa said the HE240 underwent two years of production validation at its GWh-scale manufacturing line in Fuyang, Anhui province, while the NE170 has entered batch delivery.
The company has also begun testing overseas demand. In July 2025 it delivered a 1.1 MWh sodium-ion battery cluster to a German energy company for integration into a containerized storage system. The product met IEC 62619, UN 38.3, RoHS and REACH requirements, according to HiNa.
The South Korean agreement comes amid an acceleration in sodium-ion storage commercialization in 2026.
In April, CATL and Chinese storage integrator HyperStrong signed a three-year, 60 GWh sodium-ion battery cooperation agreement, which CATL described as the world’s largest sodium-ion storage supply agreement to date.
CATL subsequently signed an agreement with Dutch energy technology company Alfen in July to deploy 5 GWh of sodium-ion storage systems across Europe, with projects expected to begin from 2027.
These agreements suggest sodium-ion batteries are beginning to move beyond pilot installations toward GWh-scale procurement, particularly in stationary storage where lower dependence on lithium resources, wide-temperature performance and high cycle capability may offer advantages. However, lithium iron phosphate remains the dominant chemistry for stationary storage, benefiting from far larger manufacturing scale and a mature supply chain. The commercial significance of HiNa Battery’s 10 GWh agreement will therefore depend on how quickly the five-year framework translates into firm project deployments and recurring deliveries in the Korean market.

title: North Macedonia’s BESS market begins to develop - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Analysis from Solar Macedonia says both standalone and co-located battery projects are beginning to materialise, while recent drought conditions have been favorable to the economic viability of solar projects.
Patrick Jowett
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
North Macedonia has begun constructing battery energy storage systems (BESS) this year, according to analysis from Macedonian solar energy association Solar Macedonia.
Professor Dimitar Dimitrov, from Skopje’s Ss. Cyril and Methodius University and Solar Macedonia, told
pv magazine
some of these projects are standalone battery storage systems, while a significant number involve the integration of battery storage to existing PV plants.
“The main objective of adding battery storage to existing PV facilities is to enable energy arbitrage by storing electricity during periods of low market prices and selling it during higher-price periods,” Dimitrov explained.
“This can improve the overall economic performance of PV projects, increase their revenues and consequently strengthen the investment case and shorten the payback period.”
Statistics from earlier in the year put North Macedonia’s installed solar capacity at
above 1 GW
. In February, the country’s Ministry of Energy, Mining and Mineral Resources approved 59 solar projects with a combined capacity over 3 GW under its 2026 annual energy construction plan. The construction plan also approved 96 energy storage facilities, including 77 integrated systems linked to new or existing plans and 19 standalone units, with a combined capacity of 2.2 GW/4.9 GWh.
Dimitrov said that during the remainder of 2026, the administrative procedures for utility-scale PV and BESS projects that are already in the national plans and have already received grid-connection approval are expected to speed up, allowing these projects to start construction in 2027.
“At the same time, C&I PV and BESS projects are expected to continue with development,” Dimitrov continued. “The main driver is the growing interest of C&I consumers in reducing their electricity costs, improving energy security and making better use of the renewable energy they produce by themselves.”
Dimitrov also said the introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which adds additional carbon-related costs to electricity exports to EU countries, is creating additional challenges, even for renewable energy investments.
“As a result, electricity producers are mainly dependent on the domestic market and on exports to non-EU countries in the region,” Dimitrov explained. “This is particularly challenging for solar PV projects. Solar generation is highest around noon hours. Consequently, in these hours electricity markets have a significant surplus of supply, leading to lower electricity prices, reducing the revenues of PV plants and making new investments less attractive.”
Dimitrov added that drought conditions and low Danube water levels that started towards the end of July have contributed to higher regional electricity prices. “[This has appeared] to be favorable for the economic viability of PV plants even in North Macedonia by increasing revenues from electricity generation,” Dimitrov told
pv magazine
Last month, Chinese construction conglomerate PowerChina was selected to implement a 30 MW solar project in North Macedonia for state-owned power utility Elektrani na Severna Makedonija (ESM).
The project, awarded through a European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) tender administered in
late 2024
, is split into two sites, a 10 MW installation at an exhausted coal mine belonging to the Oslomej thermal power plant and a 20 MW array near the Bitola thermal power plant.
Earlier this year,
pv magazine
spoke to Dimitrov about North Macedonia’s
gigawatt-sized project pipeline
of renewable energy projects during Intersolar in Munich.

title: 'It looks like there could be an undersupply of the highest efficiency' - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Alastair Mounsey, VP for Europe discusses JA’s solar moduel module strategy, why quality matters, and the growing role of energy storage in the business.
Matthew Lynas
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Module manufacturers can make money in Europe, according to JA’s new VP for the European market, despite ongoing manufacturing oversupply applying downward pressure on prices.
“The reality is that there are more modules on sale than the world needs,” Alastair Mounsey told
pv magazine.
“A lot of customers would like TOPCon 3.0 or back-contact modules, but there will not be enough of those because the machinery required to produce them represents a serious investment.”
Mounsey has worked for JA for 15 years and has been in his new post as VP for Europe since January 2026. The VP takes on the role at a time of transition for JA, which recently rebranded from JA Solar.
Change for JA has been incremental, rather than a radical departure according to Mounsey, whose own transition saw him step up from a regional sales director role responsible for the United Kingdom, Ireland, France and southeast Europe.
In addition to a new name, JA is in the middle of a manufacturing line switch from their DeepBlue 4.0 technology to their newer DeepBlue 5.0 technology. The company’s DeepBlue 4.0 modules are still in mass production, with over 40 GW capacity in June – December 2026 according to Mounsey, while JA is expected to produce over 10 GW of its DeepBlue 5.0 modules in 2026 – with the latest iteration to then account for the majority of the company’s module manufacturing in 2027.
DeepBlue 5.0 modules use the manufacturers Bycium+ 5.0 cell technology, and JA reports the latest iteration offers more power, a better temperature coefficient (-0.26%/C), and for the JAM66D50 variant, better bifaciality at 85%. The module range comprises four models, ranging from 495 W to 670 W.
Bringing a new module to market is a process that might start with R&D but the sales team plays a key role. Being comfortable with change is critical in the solar industry, where product lifecycles can be relatively short, according to Mounsey.
Alastair Mounsey, VP for Europe, JA. | Image: JA Solar
“For a PV salesperson, our job is managing change because it’s constant. It’s what we do,” he said.
That process can start early, communicating upcoming launches with distribution partners in Europe and involving regular feedback loops between the pre-sales technical team in Europe and colleagues in China. Although Mounsey acknowledged that the market only takes new product seriously once they’re fully certified to IEC standards and a PAN file exists for utility-scale simulation.
It’s necessary work, however, as next-generation, high efficiency modules are less influenced by the oversupply dynamic that is hurting the PV industry’s profits, according to Mounsey, who noted the limited number of manufacturers who have invested in lines that can produce modules offering the highest levels of efficiency.
“Let’s see what the market does, but it looks like there could be an undersupply of the highest efficiency.”
High quality is key to JA’s European strategy, Mounsey said, adding that the company has not been tempted to cut corners in to preserve margin in a low-cost environment. “We just need to get used to a low margin situation on the PV side,” he said, adding that JA’s strategy is focused on clients who demand quality. “We’re not jumping on every deal,” he said. “We provide quality products and we want quality clients.”
That requires boots on the ground, and Mounsey now heads a European team of roughly 200, covering everything but IT. The organization is split by region, not business line, and local market knowledge would seem to be key to securing volume sales in Europe.
Mounsey described Germany, Spain and the United Kingdom as core markets for JA but also highlighted Eastern and Southeastern Europe as growth markets. The Balkans and Greece may have lower volumes, but they offer potential to achieve a high market share.
Ukraine has its own distinct trajectory, Mounsey explained, with near-term PV and battery demand tied to the war and winter energy needs. However, a longer-term rebuild should come, and hopefully soon, with solar likely to play a key role.
Energy storage represents the other opportunity for the rebranded JA and here, Mounsey said the company has already made progress. JA has sought to transfer the credibility of its solar brand into the energy storage category and has already installed and commissioned projects across European countries such as the Netherlands, Italy, Germany, Ukraine and Hungary, with a pipeline in Croatia and the United Kingdom.
Roughly half of those JA energy storage sites are co-located with PV, and the rest are standalone. The co-located segment would appear to be a significant opportunity for brands offering solar and energy storage, however, as Mounsey noted that there is a clear buyer trend toward dealing with one counterparty supplier.
For the utility scale segment, JA is currently offering its JAGalaxy BESS product range which includes 5 MWh and 6.26 MWh containers, with a new generation in development. The C&I segment is served by the 261 kWh JAPlanet battery cabinet, and Mounsey reported sales volumes of the product launched in May have been strong.
“We’re selling hundreds of units of the JAPlanet,” he said.
The future for JA will to some extent involve more of the same. The manufacturer is of course keen to grow its energy business and for solar, Mounsey sees more innovation and continued incremental progress.
On the solar technology front, JA has innovated outside of its usual TOPCon patch and Mounsey highlighted the manufacturer’s HyperGen back-contact module – which set a 28.2% module efficiency record in June – as an example of innovation for the rooftop segment. But the Europe VP added he views TOPCon as the superior utility-scale technology.
“We are a TOPCon company and any back-contact type technology will only be part of the market share for us,” he said.

title: Yemen’s largest solar plant set to double to 240 MW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Yemen is expanding its largest solar power plant in Aden from 120 MW to 240 MW with UAE funding, while plans for a separate 50 MW project in Hadhramaut are also advancing. The projects form part of a growing pipeline of utility-scale solar developments across the country.
Emiliano Bellini
08 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Utility-scale
Yemen’s Minister of Electricity and Energy has announced that the country’s largest PV power plant, located in the interim capital of Aden, will be expanded with funding from the United Arab Emirates.
The agreement will add 120 MW of generation capacity to the
existing 120 MW plant
. It was signed by Yemen’s Minister of Electricity and Energy, Adnan Al-Kaf, and Ali Al Shammari, head of strategic and special projects at UAE-based renewable energy developer Masdar.
“Work on the expansion project has already begun on the ground, facilitated by the infrastructure and facilities put in place during the completion of the project’s first phase,” Al-Kaf said.
He said the second phase is expected to take approximately eight months to complete. “The additional electricity will be brought online gradually, as the transmission and distribution lines are already in place,” he said, adding that the existing power transmission infrastructure can accommodate up to 650 MW.
Masdar also built the existing 120 MW solar plant, with development starting in 2022. The expansion will bring the facility’s total installed capacity to 240 MW.
In a separate development, the government said Al-Kaf met with representatives of Maico Yemen and technical advisers to discuss plans for a 50 MW solar power plant on the Al-Qatan Plateau in Hadhramaut Governorate.
The meeting reviewed an investment proposal from Chinese electrical equipment provider Henan Longxiang, including financing and implementation mechanisms and potential partnership structures such as build-operate-transfer (BOT) and build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) models.
The ministry said the parties agreed to continue technical discussions on the project, including the potential establishment of a joint technical committee to assess its technical and economic aspects and determine the next steps toward implementation. No further details were disclosed.
Both projects are located in southern and eastern Yemen, in areas under the internationally recognized government.
Yemen currently has several PV projects under development. Chinese manufacturer TrinaSolar is partnering with local solar developer Al-Reabi on a 1.5 GW project pipeline.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), Yemen had 456 MW of operational PV capacity at the end of 2025.

title: World-first diamond quantum computer runs at -456.9°F, eyes 1,000 logical qubits
content: Japanese tech giant Fujitsu has developed the world’s first working diamond-spin quantum computer prototype that incorporates tin-vacancy (SnV) centers into photonic integrated circuits. The new prototype can run at -456.9 degrees Fahrenheit (-271.6 degrees Celsius). This is roughly 2.8 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than the -459.6 degrees Fahrenheit (-273.13 degrees Celsius) required by superconducting quantum computers. Fujitsu said that the technology could lead to more powerful quantum computers by using light to connect individual computing modules. The firm plans to create a multi-module diamond-spin prototype by 2027. It also aims to make quantum computing practical by 2030. Under its quantum roadmap, Fujitsu aims to develop a 250-logical-qubit system by fiscal 2030 and a 1,000-logical-qubit system by fiscal 2035. “We are delighted to announce this prototype diamond spin quantum computer as a result of the collaborative research conducted since 2020 between Fujitsu, Delft University of Technology, and QuTech,” Kees Eijkel, PhD, QuTech general director, pointed out. Turning diamond defects into qubits The prototype relies on lattice defects in diamond crystals, better known as color centers, to create qubits. Diamond-spin systems have typically relied on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, which are formed when a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom next to an empty position in the diamond lattice. However, for the new system, the engineers turned to tin-vacancy (SnV) centers . These defects have a tin atom positioned between two vacancies in the diamond structure. Fujitsu said that their symmetrical structure makes SnV centers less susceptible to external noise than conventional NV centers. Additionally, SnV centers emit light at roughly 10 times the brightness of NV centers. This could potentially improve the optical connections between quantum modules. The approach could also lead to more efficient error correction. Its properties can keep quantum states stable, and allow logical qubits (groups of physical qubits that run quantum computations using specifications of a quantum algorithm) to be formed with fewer physical qubits than competing methods. Quantum links using light For the system, Fujitsu first created a process to bond high-quality, tin-implanted diamond substrates to alumina and silicon dioxide substrates. The diamond was thinned from several hundred micrometers to just several hundred nanometers for integration into quantum chips. It also made photonic integrated circuits that combine nanometer-sized diamond crystals containing SnV centers with alumina optical waveguides. Finally, it created a mechanism to control the diamond-spin qubits with light, microwaves, as well as radio-frequency waves. “The diamond-spin approach we have applied in this prototype not only offers exceptional scalability in its own right, but also has the potential to be integrated with superconducting quantum computers to further extend their capabilities, enabling more complex and large-scale computations,” Vivek Mahajan, Fujitsu’s CTO, said. The device has already been operated in a test environment through the Fujitsu Hybrid Quantum Computing Platform. Users do not need additional specialist knowledge to control the new hardware, according to the company. “Under our roadmap to achieve a 250 logical qubit system by fiscal 2030 and a 1,000 logical qubit system by fiscal 2035, Fujitsu will continue advancing practical quantum computing across a broad range of areas, from software to hardware, while leveraging the key advantages of the diamond-spin approach, including high fidelity and optical connectivity,” Mahajan concluded in a statement .

title: X-59: US supersonic aircraft hits Mach 1.2 at 49,000 feet in 25th test flight
content: NASA’s X-59 experimental supersonic aircraft has successfully completed 25 test flights. It reached Mach 1.2 at 49,000 feet and validated key predictions regarding stability, flying qualities, and structural loads. Rather than the speed itself, the flight’s true success lay in how quietly it passed over the desert floor. Designed to trade the deafening crack of supersonic travel for a gentle, barely noticeable “thump,” the needle-nosed aircraft is meeting every single performance mark set by its engineering team. These trials clear the way for NASA to begin measuring the jet’s acoustic signature later this year. “Through our ongoing flight tests with the X-59, we’ve gained invaluable insights into both the aircraft’s performance and the unique challenges of the aircraft design,” said Cathy Bahm, project manager for NASA’s Low Boom Flight Demonstrator project. “Each test point has validated our models and predictions, and it has strengthened our confidence in the aircraft’s performance. Every flight brings us closer to transitioning to the next phase where we will demonstrate the X-59’s quiet supersonic flight capabilities.” Use of computer modeling Building a jet meant to defy decades of acoustic limits requires equal parts hubris and hyper-precise computer modeling. Before construction began, NASA engineers developed a virtual “digital twin” to simulate the X-59’s flight dynamics. Today, real-time sensor data from actual test flights is validating those early computer models with accuracy. The X-59 has passed several crucial design checks. Flight controls remain smooth and responsive under high stress. Aerodynamic forces stay within safe limits without twisting the airframe. The top-mounted inlet also reliably feeds air to the GE-F414 engine during maneuvers. Tests show no unexpected vibration, flutter, or instability. NASA test pilots describe the flights as remarkably smooth, allowing engineers to focus on evaluating performance across the aircraft’s full operational range. In fact, NASA test pilot Nils Larson described flying the cutting-edge experimental jet as “exciting but uneventful.” Every test flight builds on past data to refine control software and resolve minor sensor glitches. Key components, such as the single GE-F414 engine’ s top-mounted air inlet, have performed reliably across diverse flight conditions. These successful trials set the stage for the Quesst mission’s main objective: evaluating how the X-59 actually sounds at supersonic cruise speeds. The real test lies ahead While the X-59 has already hit its cruise targets of Mach 1.4 and 55,000 feet, previous flights relied on conventional chase planes whose own roaring sonic booms masked the experimental jet’s sound signature The mission will soon enter its crucial acoustic validation phase. Researchers will deploy ground sensors and airborne microphones to measure the aircraft’s shockwaves. This data will reveal the exact acoustic footprint of the X-59’s supersonic flight. “Acoustic validation will put the tools and methods used to design the X-59 to the test — tools that could ultimately become part of the DNA of every future commercial supersonic aircraft,” said Larry Cliatt, acoustic validation technical lead for NASA’s Quesst mission. “It will be a complex and demanding flight campaign focused on demonstrating that the X-59 can produce the quiet sonic thump it was designed to achieve.” If those ground tests show the jet’s acoustic thump is soft enough for suburban skies, NASA plans to fly the X-59 over several US communities to gather public feedback. This data could persuade regulators to lift the long-standing ban on overland commercial supersonic flight. Eliminating the ban would pave the way for airliners that cut travel times in half without disturbing people on the ground.

title: China studies underground farming in its abandoned coal mines
content: China could turn thousands of abandoned coal mines into underground agricultural laboratories, using the vast spaces and existing infrastructure left behind by the country’s mining industry to explore farming in controlled environments.Researchers from the Shanxi Province Coal-based Resources Green and High-efficiency Development Engineering Center outlined the proposal in a recent paper published in China Mining Magazine. They argue that abandoned mines could provide a stable environment for studying “closed-environment farming” as climate change makes conventional agriculture increasingly vulnerable.Farming beneath the surfaceAccording to South China Morning Post (SCMP) China is expected to have around 15,000 abandoned mines by 2030, creating enormous amounts of unused underground space. Researchers estimate that the volume could reach about 7.2 billion cubic meters (254 billion cubic feet).Unlike conventional farmland, underground tunnels are largely insulated from seasonal temperature changes and many weather-related hazards. The researchers believe this could make them useful for controlled agricultural experiments, where conditions such as temperature, light, water and air can be precisely managed.The lack of sunlight is an obvious challenge, but the researchers argue that existing electrical infrastructure at abandoned mines could support artificial lighting systems. Underground temperatures also fluctuate far less than those at the surface, potentially reducing the energy required to maintain suitable growing conditions.Geothermal energy could provide another advantage, potentially supplying heat for underground cultivation while reducing reliance on fossil fuels.The researchers are not proposing that abandoned mines immediately become giant underground farms. Instead, they envisage them primarily as agricultural engineering experimental platforms where scientists can investigate how crops respond to controlled underground environments.An opportunity to deal with mine waterThe proposal could also provide another use for infrastructure left behind by the mining industry: treating contaminated mine water. Abandoned mines can contain residual pollutants, including lubricating oils and hydraulic fluids. Contaminated water can also migrate through geological faults, cracks and poorly sealed boreholes, potentially reaching surface water.The researchers suggest that underground agricultural laboratories could provide a practical reason to develop systems for treating and reusing this water. Water containing high concentrations of sulfates or heavy-metal ions could undergo processes such as adsorption and membrane separation before being used for suitable crops.They cite acid-tolerant plants including rapeseed and tea as potential candidates. This could create a circular system in which infrastructure, energy and water resources associated with abandoned mines are reused rather than simply left to deteriorate.From abandoned mines to space farmsThe researchers also see a more unusual application for the technology. By creating controlled ecosystems deep underground, scientists could study how plants respond when natural environmental conditions are removed or tightly controlled. The resulting knowledge could eventually contribute to long-duration space missions, where reliable food production would be essential but natural sunlight, soil and stable environmental conditions cannot be assumed. China has already begun experimenting with the concept.In Daye, Hubei province, researchers have been growing butterhead lettuce about 245 meters (804 feet) underground inside an abandoned copper mine. The facility uses artificial lighting, intelligent cultivation systems and low-carbon energy to maintain the crops. Similar experiments are taking place elsewhere. In Britain’s North Yorkshire, researchers have established an underground farming facility more than 1,000 meters below ground to test how crops can be cultivated deep beneath the surface.The concept is not new. British researcher Saffa Riffat proposed using abandoned coal mines for underground agriculture as early as 2018, arguing that such spaces could help address growing food demand while giving former mining infrastructure a new purpose.For China, however, the scale of the opportunity is particularly large. The country has already closed around 12,000 mines between 2010 and 2019, and thousands more are expected to shut down in the coming years.Rather than allowing those tunnels to become another legacy of the coal industry, researchers believe they could become laboratories for a different kind of agriculture. One designed to operate independently of the increasingly unpredictable environment
